Class GraphObjectFrame

java.lang.Object
ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, CanvasItem
public class GraphObjectFrame extends Object implements Serializable, CanvasItem
The frame that marks out one Petri-object on the canvas.

A Petri-object is not a separate drawing: it is a named region of the one canvas, and whatever belongs to it is drawn inside it. That keeps the structure of a model and the behaviour of its objects in a single picture — a token crossing a frame border is a token crossing an object border.

Which elements those are is decided once - grouped into the frame, drawn on the object's own canvas, dragged in and confirmed, or loaded as part of it - and stays exactly that set of elements afterward, independent of the frame's own position: GraphCanvasModel.claim(ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphObjectFrame, ua.stetsenkoinna.graphnet.GraphElement) is the only thing that puts an element in this object, so moving the frame across the canvas can never by itself hand it something it was never given. The member set is deliberately written only from GraphCanvasModel, which is what makes "exactly one frame claims an element" a structural guarantee instead of a convention every caller has to remember.

A frame can also sit inside another frame, which is what nesting one Petri-object in another means. That is a frame-to-frame relation (getEnclosing()), never membership: members only ever holds places and transitions, so an enclosing object's own member set says nothing about the objects nested in it.

Collapsing a frame shrinks it down to a small node, for when a model has grown past what fits on screen — a distinct, coarser thing from the eye icon in the header, which only ever hides the net's drawing without changing the frame's own size: what a collapsed frame does to its footprint on the canvas, the eye does to what is painted inside that footprint. Either way an object's own places and transitions still exist and still hold their marking; hiding them is a drawing choice, not a structural one, which is also why a locked object still reaches the rest of the model through its ports regardless of whether its content is shown.

    • GraphObjectFrame

    • GraphObjectFrame

      public GraphObjectFrame(GraphObjectFrame other, Map<GraphElement,GraphElement> oldToNew)
      Copies another frame's own state — bounds, name, priority, template, collapsed and content-visibility — and translates its membership through oldToNew so the copy claims the corresponding NEW element instances rather than the ones other claims. collapsed/expandedBounds are copied as plain field values rather than replayed through setCollapsed(boolean), which computes a derived rectangle and would get the wrong answer fed a bounds/collapsed pair that do not match its own transition history.
      Parameters:
      other - the frame to copy

      enclosing is deliberately NOT translated here: the frame it would point at may not have been copied yet, so GraphCanvasModel's own copy constructor wires every copy's parent in a second pass once all of them exist.

      oldToNew - maps every element other might claim to its already-made copy; a member with no entry is dropped rather than left dangling on the original
      other - the frame to copy

    • getExpandedBounds

      public Rectangle getExpandedBounds()
      Returns:
      the rectangle this frame occupies when expanded: its bounds as they are, or, while collapsed, the remembered expanded ones. This is what persistence has to write: saving a collapsed frame's summary-box rectangle as its size meant the reloaded object expanded into a box smaller than the minimum a user could ever resize one to, with its whole net piled inside.

    • isContentShown

      public boolean isContentShown()
      Returns:
      true if this object's own net is actually on screen right now — both the eye icon has it shown and the frame is not collapsed, since a collapsed frame hides everything regardless of what the eye says. The one thing to check before reaching for a place or transition directly instead of through its port.

    • moveTo

      public void moveTo(int x, int y)
      Moves the frame, keeping its size. The remembered expanded rectangle travels by the same delta: it used to stay behind, so dragging a collapsed object and expanding it snapped the frame back to where it was collapsed while its net, carried by the drag, stayed at the drop point - frame and net permanently separated.

    • moveBy

      public void moveBy(int dx, int dy)
      Moves this frame alone by a delta - never its nested subtree or the elements it claims, the same restriction CanvasItem.moveBy(int, int) documents. A drag that must cascade to those still goes through moveTo directly the way it always did, one call per item in the subtree, since only GraphCanvasModel knows what that subtree is.
      Specified by:
      moveBy in interface CanvasItem
      Parameters:
      dx - horizontal shift, in canvas coordinates
      dy - vertical shift, in canvas coordinates
